pos: n. (proper name; a priest who sealed Nehemiah's covenant)
etymology: Hebrew Bilgai, apparently a variant of Bilgah, from a root suggesting cheerfulness or brightening. Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 12 carry the related priestly name Bilgah.
biblical_def: Bilgai is named once: “Maaziah, Bilgai, Shemaiah: these were the priests” (Nehemiah 10:8). The verse closes the list of twenty-one priests who set their seals to the document of Nehemiah 10, and that document is one of the most remarkable acts in the Old Testament. After the law had been read aloud for days and the people had stood and confessed, the nation did not merely feel: it signed. “And because of all this we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it” (Nehemiah 9:38). Then come four chapters' worth of names, and after the names the specific obligations — no intermarriage with the peoples of the land, no trading on the sabbath, the seventh-year release, a fixed levy for the house of God, the firstfruits, the tithes. Bilgai is a name on a legal instrument. The dictionary marks the shape of this repentance, because it is the pattern Scripture commends: conviction that proceeds to written, dated, specific commitment. Feeling that never reaches an obligation has not yet repented of anything.

So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Repentance is reduced to sentiment; Nehemiah's people wrote theirs down, sealed it, and listed the obligations.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religious feeling is suspicious of written commitments, preferring sincerity to subscription, and the result is a piety that resolves nothing. Nehemiah 9 and 10 show the alternative. The people were moved — they wept, confessed, and stood a quarter of the day under the reading — and then they drew up a document, sealed it with named men's seals, and enumerated exactly what they would and would not do.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that genuine repentance becomes concrete. It names the sin, names the remedy, and binds the conscience before witnesses. The confessional churches follow Nehemiah 10 when they subscribe a written standard, and a conviction that will not be written down is usually a conviction that intends to change nothing.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite who sealed Nehemiah's covenant)
etymology: Hebrew Beninu, commonly read our son, from ben (son) with the first-person plural suffix. The form is a sentence-name, as many Hebrew names are.
biblical_def: Beninu is named once, and his verse is three words long: “Hodijah, Bani, Beninu” (Nehemiah 10:13). He closes the roll of Levites who sealed the covenant. His name means our son, which is a parent's word rather than a description of the man, and it is the only thing Scripture tells us besides his office and his signature. The dictionary draws attention to the office. The Levites in these chapters are doing the work the law gave them: they read the book distinctly and gave the sense (Nehemiah 8:8), they led the confession from the stairs, and here they bind themselves by seal along with the priests and princes. A reformation in Israel ran through teachers. The people could not have repented of what they had not understood, and they could not have understood without men who stood up and explained the text. Beninu is one name at the end of a list of such men. He taught, and he signed what he taught, and the second is the proof of the first.

corruption_summary: Reformation is credited to movements and moods; in Nehemiah it ran through men who explained the text.
corruption_paragraphs: Revivals are commonly narrated as surges of feeling that arise and subside. Nehemiah 8 describes the mechanism differently: men read the law distinctly, gave the sense, and caused the people to understand the reading. The weeping came after the understanding, and the covenant came after the weeping. The order is not accidental.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the primacy of plain teaching. Where the Scriptures are read and explained, consciences are reached; where they are not, no amount of atmosphere will substitute. The Levites who gave the sense are the same men who sealed the obligations, and Beninu's name at the foot of the document is a teacher putting himself under his own lesson.

pos: n. (proper name; one of those who put away strange wives in Ezra's reformation)
etymology: Hebrew Bedeyah, apparently a shortened form meaning servant of the LORD, with the divine element -yah closing the name.
biblical_def: Bedeiah is named once, in a list that cost every man on it dearly: “Benaiah, Bedeiah, Chelluh” (Ezra 10:35). Ezra 10 is the register of those who had married wives from the peoples of the land and who, upon the reading of the law, put them away. It is among the hardest chapters in the Old Testament, and the dictionary will not soften it or pretend it is simple. The men themselves proposed the remedy: “Now therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all the wives, and such as are born of them … and let it be done according to the law” (Ezra 10:3). The issue was not ethnicity — Ruth the Moabitess is in the line of David, and Rahab of Jericho with her — but covenant. These were marriages to women who served other gods, contracted by the remnant God had just brought back from a seventy-year judgment for precisely that sin. Ezra's prayer sets the terms: “O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee” (Ezra 9:6). Bedeiah is a name among men who took their own sin seriously enough to let it hurt them.

corruption_summary: Ezra 10 is read as ethnic purging; the issue throughout is covenant loyalty, not blood.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 10 is routinely condemned as racial exclusion, and the charge collapses on the Bible's own evidence. Scripture places a Moabitess and a Canaanite woman of Jericho in the genealogy of Christ and honours both; Israel was commanded to love the stranger within her gates. What Ezra confronted was marriage into the worship of other gods by the very remnant whose exile had been the judgment for that worship.

The principle to recover is that covenant fidelity cuts deeper than natural affection, and that God's remedies are sometimes severe. The dictionary does not pretend the chapter is painless; it records that the men themselves proposed the separation, trembling at the commandment, and that the alternative was the loss of the remnant's children to the gods of the land — which is exactly what Nehemiah found happening a generation later.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite dwelling in Jerusalem after the return)
etymology: Hebrew Baqbaqqar, of uncertain meaning; a connection with a root for searching out or investigating has been proposed, as has one with a word for a bottle or flask.
biblical_def: Bakbakkar is named once: “And Bakbakkar, Heresh, and Galal, and Mattaniah the son of Micah, the son of Zichri, the son of Asaph” (1 Chronicles 9:15). The chapter is the Chronicler's register of who lived in Jerusalem after the captivity — priests, Levites, singers, porters — and it is a quietly magnificent list. The city had been burned, the walls broken down, the temple levelled; and here is a roll of the men who came back to live in it and to do the work of the house of God. The Chronicler describes them in a phrase worth memorising: “very able men for the work of the service of the house of God” (1 Chronicles 9:13). Bakbakkar belongs to the Asaphite line of singers, and so his work was praise. The dictionary notes what that meant in context. A man whose office is to sing in a ruined city is making a confession about the future: that there will be a house, that it will be served, and that God is worth praising in the rubble. Those who returned were not sentimentalists; they were men who believed a promise and moved back.

corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of contemporary worship assumes that praise follows favourable conditions, so that singing is the natural overflow of a settled and comfortable people. The register of 1 Chronicles 9 is a list of singers assigned to a city still largely in ruins, employed in that work day and night. The exiles had asked how they could sing the LORD's song in a strange land; the answer when they came home was that they would sing it in a wrecked one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship rests on God's character and not on our circumstances. He was no less worthy among the broken walls than He had been in Solomon's courts, and the men who understood that are the ones the Chronicler calls very able for the work of the service of the house of God.

pos: n. (proper name; father of one who repaired the old gate of Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Besodeyah, commonly read in the counsel of the LORD or in the secret of the LORD, from sod (counsel, secret) with the divine element -yah.
biblical_def: Besodeiah is named once, and only as a father: “Moreover the old gate repaired Jehoiada the son of Paseah, and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah; they laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, and the locks thereof, and the bars thereof” (Nehemiah 3:6). His son Meshullam worked on the old gate, and the verse records the work in carpenter's detail — beams, doors, locks, bars. Nehemiah 3 is the chapter of names and sections: the priests built by the sheep gate, the goldsmiths and the apothecaries took a stretch, the daughters of Shallum helped their father, one man repaired over against his own house. Forty-odd parties, each with a measured piece, and the wall finished in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). That is what the chapter is for. Besodeiah's name means in the counsel of the LORD, and the counsel of the LORD in that generation was a wall; and the way it came about was that a great many ordinary people each took the section in front of them. The dictionary commends the arrangement. Nobody built the wall. Everybody built a piece of it, and the wall got built.

corruption_paragraphs: The habit of attributing accomplishment to a single visionary figure would make Nehemiah 3 unnecessary, and the chapter exists to prevent it. The book names the goldsmiths, the apothecaries, the merchants, the Tekoites, the daughters of Shallum, and dozens of householders who repaired the piece of wall in front of their own doors. Nehemiah organised it; the people built it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity and sufficiency of ordinary labour rightly directed. “So built we the wall … for the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6). Fifty-two days is what happens when a whole city takes the section in front of it, and Besodeiah is in Scripture because his son took one gate.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite name borne by more than one man after the return)
etymology: Hebrew Bunni, from a root meaning to build, with the sense built or my building — the same root that gives ben, a son, since a son is how a house is built up.
biblical_def: Bunni occurs three times, and the occurrences belong to more than one man. A Levite stood with others on the stairs in the great confession: “Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God” (Nehemiah 9:4). A chief of the people sealed the covenant: “Bunni, Azgad, Bebai” (Nehemiah 10:15). And a third is named as an ancestor: “Shemaiah the son of Hashub, the son of Azrikam, the son of Hashabiah, the son of Bunni” (Nehemiah 11:15). The dictionary treats the name as one entry and the men as distinct, which is what the text supports. The root is worth dwelling on: Bunni is from the verb to build. These are the generations of the rebuilding — of a wall, of a temple, of a people — and a man named built cried with a loud voice to the LORD on the stairs while the city rose around him. The names of that generation keep saying the same thing, because God was doing one thing: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psalm 127:1).

corruption_paragraphs: The restoration under Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah is naturally read as a construction project with political backing, and so it was. But the books themselves keep assigning the work elsewhere: the LORD stirred up Cyrus, the LORD put it into Nehemiah's heart, the eye of their God was upon the elders. The men built, and they did not consider themselves the builders.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is stated in one verse: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psalm 127:1). It does not excuse idleness — the wall went up in fifty-two days of hard work — but it settles the question of whose wall it was. A man named built crying to God from the stairs had the matter in the right order.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the sons of Bebai in Ezra's reformation)
etymology: Hebrew 'Athlai, generally taken as a shortened form of a name compounded with the divine element, perhaps the LORD is exalted. The full form is not preserved.
biblical_def: Athlai is named once: “Of the sons also of Bebai; Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai” (Ezra 10:28). He stands in the register of Ezra 10, the list of men who had married wives from the peoples of the land and who put them away when the law was pressed upon them. Four brothers of one house are named together here, which is worth noticing: the sin ran in families, and so did the repentance. The dictionary records what the chapter records, including its difficulty. Ezra had torn his garment and plucked out his hair and sat down astonished; the people gathered and wept very sore; and the proposal to separate came from among the people themselves, from those who, in the chapter's own phrase, tremble at the commandment of our God (Ezra 10:3). Four sons of Bebai are in that number. There is no way to read Ezra 10 as cheap. Every name on the list is a man who did something that hurt him because the law of God required it, and the register exists so that the cost would be remembered along with the obedience.

corruption_paragraphs: A religion of self-fulfilment cannot read Ezra 10, because the chapter records obedience that cost its men their households. The dictionary does not blunt it. The point of the register is that these men are named — the record keeps the price alongside the names, and the congregation's answer was given with a loud voice: as thou hast said, so must we do.

The principle to recover is that the commandment of God is not negotiated down to what we can bear comfortably. Those who acted were described as men who tremble at the commandment of our God, and that trembling, not enthusiasm, is what carried the reformation. A church that has lost the category of costly obedience has lost the category these men lived in.

pos: n. (proper name; father of a ruler of half Bethzur who repaired the wall)
etymology: Hebrew 'Azbuq, of uncertain meaning; a connection with a root for strength ('az) has been proposed, the second element remaining obscure.
biblical_def: Azbuk is named once, as a father: “After him repaired Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, the ruler of the half part of Bethzur, unto the place over against the sepulchres of David, and to the pool that was made, and unto the house of the mighty” (Nehemiah 3:16). His son Nehemiah is not the Nehemiah of the book — that one is the son of Hachaliah — but a different man of the same name, a district official from Bethzur some miles south of Jerusalem who came up and took a section of wall. The dictionary notes the detail because it is easy to misread and because of what it shows. The rebuilding was not done by Jerusalemites alone. Men came from Tekoa, from Gibeon, from Mizpah, from Jericho, from Zanoah and from Bethzur, each with a stretch assigned, leaving their own towns to work on someone else's wall. The section this Nehemiah took ran past the tombs of the kings. A provincial ruler spent his season laying stone over against the sepulchres of David — which is a picture of the whole enterprise: men of the present repairing a city for the sake of promises made to the dead and to be kept to the unborn.

Patronymics exist precisely so that common names can be told apart, and the record supplies them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the work of God draws in people with no local stake. Men came from half a dozen towns to build a wall they would not live behind. Nehemiah 3:5 records the opposite case in the same chapter — the Tekoite nobles who put not their necks to the work of their Lord — so the reader may see both the willing and the unwilling named on the same page.

pos: n. (proper name; father of the Levite Jeshua who sealed the covenant)
etymology: Hebrew 'Azanyah, commonly read the LORD hath heard, from a root meaning to give ear or hearken, with the divine element -yah.
biblical_def: Azaniah is named once, as a father: “And the Levites: both Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel” (Nehemiah 10:9). The verse heads the Levites' portion of the sealed covenant, and his son Jeshua is the first of them named. The name is a confession: the LORD hath heard. Set it against the chapter before, where the Levites stood on the stairs and cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God, and against the long prayer of Nehemiah 9 that recites the whole history of Israel's rebellion and God's patience and ends “we make a sure covenant, and write it” (Nehemiah 9:38). A generation that had come back from Babylon bore names like this one because they had evidence for it. Their fathers had prayed in exile and been brought home. The dictionary marks how Hebrew naming works: a man's name was often a sentence of theology spoken over him by parents who meant it, and a roll of such names is a kind of creed. The Levite who signed the covenant was the son of a man called the LORD hath heard, and the signing was the proof.

corruption_summary: Biblical names are treated as arbitrary labels; in Hebrew they are commonly sentences of theology spoken over a child.
corruption_paragraphs: Names in Scripture are frequently passed over as noise between the events, which flattens whole chapters into lists. Hebrew naming is confessional: the LORD hath heard, the LORD is my God, built, in the counsel of the LORD. A register of restoration-era names is a record of what that generation believed about God, repeated in every household.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that parents teach doctrine by what they put on their children and in their mouths. “I love the LORD, because he hath heard my voice and my supplications” (Psalm 116:1) is the sentiment Azaniah's name carries, and his son put his seal to a written covenant with the God his father had named him after.

pos: n. (proper name; a musician at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew 'Azar'el, God hath helped, from 'azar (to help) and 'el (God). The Authorized Version spells the same name Azareel elsewhere.
biblical_def: Azarael is named once, in the procession at the dedication of the wall: “And his brethren, Shemaiah, and Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, and Judah, Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God, and Ezra the scribe before them” (Nehemiah 12:36). His name means God hath helped, and he is holding one of the instruments of David at the moment the city's restoration was celebrated. Nehemiah 12 is the one unambiguously joyful chapter in the book. Two great companies of singers went in opposite directions along the top of the finished wall and met at the house of God, and the verse that closes the scene is among the gladdest in the Old Testament: “Also that day they offered great sacrifices, and rejoiced: for God had made them rejoice with great joy: the wives also and the children rejoiced: so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off” (Nehemiah 12:43). A man named God hath helped played David's instruments on a wall that had been a heap of burnt stone. The dictionary notes that the joy is credited where the help was: God made them rejoice. Even the gladness of that day was a gift and not an achievement.

And at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought the Levites out of all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem, to keep the dedication with gladness, both with thanksgivings, and with singing, with cymbals, psalteries, and with harps.

Also that day they offered great sacrifices, and rejoiced: for God had made them rejoice with great joy: the wives also and the children rejoiced: so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off.

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
corruption_summary: Joy is treated as a mood the worshipper must manufacture; Nehemiah credits it to God, who made them rejoice.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary worship often places the burden of gladness on the worshipper, as something to be worked up and sustained. Nehemiah 12:43 assigns it elsewhere in so many words: they rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy. The singers were sought out, the instruments were David's, the sacrifices were offered — and the joy itself was His doing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that joy is a fruit and a gift, not an atmosphere. “The joy of the LORD is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10) runs the other way from how it is usually quoted: the strength comes from His joy, not from ours. A man called God hath helped, playing on a rebuilt wall, is the right picture of it.
